beats.lead: Fleming spotted it. Someone else made it a medicine.
beats.text: Fleming saw the mould killing bacteria in 1928. A team in Oxford turned it into a drug.
beats.note: His 1929 paper drew little attention. Florey, Chain and colleagues showed it killed bacteria in living bodies as well as in dishes.

beats.name: Albert Alexander
beats.role: Oxford police officer and the first patient given penicillin, on 12 February 1941. He improved, then the supply ran out and he died.

beats.text: The mould grew as a thin film, so output stayed tiny.
beats.note: Corn steep liquor, a cheap corn belt by-product, and a better strain found on a mouldy fruit in a Peoria market made large scale production possible.

beats.text: 2.3 million doses had been made in time for the Normandy landings.
beats.note: Allied soldiers carried the antibiotic onto the beaches on 6 June 1944.

beats.context: Units of penicillin a year being made in the United States by June 1945.
